title: Usage in the Real World
bigQuestion: If the rules of English keep changing and vary from one room to the next, how does a writer know which ones to follow, and when?

story.title: Sixty Letters and One Word
story.kicker: A hiring manager reads a stack of cover letters on a Friday afternoon, and one of them ends before the second sentence.
paragraphs: Priya Nair runs the summer internship program at an architecture firm in Chicago's West Loop. Every March she gets about sixty applications for four spots, and every March she reads the cover letters on a single Friday afternoon with a cup of coffee and a rule she does not enjoy: she reads until she finds a reason to stop. Sixty letters, four hours. The rule is not cruelty. It is arithmetic.

Marcus Bell's letter was the twenty-third. He had a strong transcript, a drafting portfolio from a community college class, and a summer of framing houses with his uncle. His first sentence was fine. His second sentence read, "I would be a real asset to you're team because I pay attention to the details other people miss." Priya read it twice. Then she put the letter on the pile to the left, the pile that would get the polite form email, and picked up the twenty-fourth.

Marcus found out why only because Priya's assistant, who had gone to his high school, told him. The word was not the problem, exactly. Priya would not have noticed you're for your in a text message, and she knew perfectly well what he meant. The problem was that the sentence claimed to notice details in the same breath that it missed one, in a letter that had been written to be judged, for a job in which a misplaced number on a drawing can cost a client a wall. The letter had one job: to show that its writer could be trusted with small things. One word made the letter argue against itself.

Marcus rewrote it, read it aloud, asked two people to read it, and sent it to another firm, which hired him. He kept the old letter. He says the mistake taught him something no grammar worksheet ever had: in the real world, usage is not a test with a score. It is a signal that a reader uses to decide, in seconds, whether to keep reading. This chapter is about those signals, where they come from, why they change, and how to send the ones you mean to send.
story.think: Priya admits she would have ignored the same error in a text. Is it fair to judge a person's care by one word in a letter, and does fairness change what Marcus should do next time?

lessons.title: Prescriptive and Descriptive
lessons.mainIdea: Prescriptive rules tell writers what they should do; descriptive study records what speakers and writers actually do; a skilled writer uses both.
reading: Two people look at the sentence "Me and him went to the store." The first says, "That is wrong; it should be He and I went." The second says, "Millions of English speakers say it that way every day, so it is part of English." Both are right about something. The first is speaking *prescriptively*, stating a rule about what writers should do. The second is speaking *descriptively*, reporting what speakers actually do. Grammar books are mostly prescriptive. Linguists, the scientists who study language, are mostly descriptive. The two groups have argued for two hundred years, and the argument is worth understanding because you will live inside it.

The descriptive view rests on a fact: language changes, and no rulebook has ever stopped it. English once had the word thou, and every dictionary lost it. Rules that were once fiercely enforced, such as never using the word contact as a verb, are now forgotten. A descriptivist notices that "Me and him went" follows a perfectly regular pattern that many speakers share, and that calling it wrong is really calling it nonstandard, which means outside the variety of English that schools and employers expect. That variety, *Standard English*, is not more logical than the others. It is the one with power behind it.

The prescriptive view rests on a different fact: readers judge. Priya did not care whether you're for your was a natural variation. She cared that the letter was for a job. When you write for school, for work, for a grant or for a court, your reader expects Standard English, and a rule that says "use it here" is not snobbery but advice about the room you are in. The best writers hold both views at once. They know the rules, they know which rules are really just habits, and they know that following the expected rules is a courtesy to the reader that costs the writer nothing.

A *usage* question, then, is rarely "is this correct?" It is "is this what this reader, in this setting, expects?" That reframing will get you through most of the disputes in this chapter. It also tells you what to do when a rule seems silly: follow it where a reader expects it, drop it where no one does, and be able to say why.

words.d: describing rules that state how language should be used
describing the study of how language actually is used by speakers and writers
the variety of English expected in schools, workplaces and formal writing
the way words and constructions are actually used, and the customs about which uses are accepted where

look.title: Two Notes on One Sentence
look.text: A teacher writes "nonstandard" beside "Me and him went" on a student's essay. A linguist reading the same sentence writes "regular pattern: object pronouns in a compound subject, widespread in spoken American English." Both notes are accurate.
look.prompt: What does each note tell the student to do, and what would a note that used both views say?

check.q: What does a descriptive approach to language do?
choices: Records how people actually use language
Tells writers which forms to use
Bans nonstandard forms
Decides which words enter the dictionary by vote
check.why: Descriptive study observes and reports usage rather than ruling on it.

check.q: According to the lesson, what makes Standard English standard?
choices: It is the most logical variety
It is the variety with institutional power behind it, expected in schools and workplaces
It is the oldest form of English
It has the fewest words
check.why: Standard English is not more logical than other varieties; it is the one that schools and employers expect.

check.q: How does the lesson reframe the question "Is this correct?"
choices: Is this the oldest form?
Would a linguist approve?
Is this what this reader, in this setting, expects?
Does the dictionary list it?
check.why: Usage depends on reader and setting, which is why both views matter.

lessons.title: Rules That Changed
lessons.mainIdea: Several famous rules, including the bans on split infinitives, sentence-ending prepositions and singular they, were never solid, and today's major guides have loosened or dropped them.
reading: "She decided to quietly leave." For more than a century, teachers marked that sentence wrong because an adverb sits between to and leave, splitting the *infinitive*. The rule appeared in the 1800s, when some grammarians modeled English on Latin, where an infinitive is one word and cannot be split. English is not Latin. Writers had been splitting infinitives since the 1300s, and every major American style guide now says the split is fine when it reads more naturally. "She decided quietly to leave" is stiff and slightly unclear; the split version is better.

The ban on ending a sentence with a *preposition* has the same history and the same fate. "Where are you from?" is normal English; "From where are you?" is nobody's speech. A related rule said never to begin a sentence with and or but. Good writers have always done it, and doing it is often the clearest way to mark a turn. None of these was ever a rule of English grammar. Each was a rule of taste that some people mistook for a law.

The newest change is *singular they*. English has no common pronoun for one person of unknown or unstated gender, and for centuries writers filled the gap with they: "Someone left their umbrella." Shakespeare did it, and so did Jane Austen. Grammarians of the 1800s pushed "he" as the generic pronoun, and schools taught it until the late twentieth century. The guides have since reversed. The Associated Press Stylebook permitted limited singular they in 2017, the Chicago Manual of Style's seventeenth edition (2017) accepted it in speech and informal writing, and the APA manual's seventh edition (2019) endorsed it in all writing. Merriam-Webster named "they" its Word of the Year for 2019. Singular they also serves people who use it as their personal pronoun, and using a person's stated pronoun is now standard courtesy in most workplaces.

The lesson is not that rules do not matter. It is that a rule has a history, and knowing the history lets you follow it or set it aside on purpose. If you split an infinitive in a college paper, no careful reader will blink. If you write "Each student must bring their own laptop," the APA will nod. But an older reader, or a very formal setting, may still expect the old forms, and you can choose to give them what they expect. That choice, made knowingly, is what fluency looks like.

words.d: the base form of a verb with to, as in to leave; splitting it means placing a word between to and the verb
a word such as from, with or about that shows a relationship, often between a noun and the rest of the sentence
the use of they, them or their to refer to one person, as in Someone left their umbrella
a pronoun used to refer to any person in general rather than a particular one

look.title: The Guides Move on Singular They
rows: Chicago Manual, 17th ed., accepts in informal writing
APA manual, 7th ed., endorses in all writing
Merriam-Webster names they Word of the Year
look.cite: publication dates of the guides and the dictionary's annual announcement
look.prompt: Four major authorities shifted within three years after centuries of use. What does that timing suggest about who leads a change in usage, the guides or the speakers?

check.q: Why did the rule against splitting infinitives arise?
choices: Because English infinitives are one word
Because split infinitives are always unclear
Because the Associated Press banned them
Because some grammarians in the 1800s modeled English on Latin, where an infinitive cannot be split
check.why: The rule copied Latin grammar; English writers had split infinitives for centuries before it appeared.

check.q: What does the lesson say about "Where are you from?"
choices: It is normal English, and the rule against ending with a preposition was a matter of taste
It is wrong and should be From where are you?
It is acceptable only in speech
It is a comma splice
check.why: The preposition rule was never a law of English grammar.

check.q: Which statement about singular they is supported by the reading?
choices: It was invented in 2017
It has centuries of use, and the major guides accepted it between 2017 and 2019
No style guide accepts it
Shakespeare refused to use it
check.why: Writers including Shakespeare and Austen used it, and AP, Chicago and APA accepted it in 2017–2019.

lessons.title: Usage Still Argued Today
lessons.mainIdea: Some usage questions, such as less versus fewer, who versus whom, and literally as an intensifier, remain genuinely contested, and the writer's best move is to know the dispute and choose for the reader.
reading: The grocery sign says "10 items or less." A certain kind of reader winces and wants "fewer," because the traditional rule says fewer for things you count (fewer coins) and less for things you measure (less money). Dictionaries note that less with countable nouns has been in use for a thousand years, and "10 items or less" bothers almost no shopper. Still, in a college paper or a job application, "fewer" is the safe choice, because the reader who winces might be the one grading. This is the pattern of a *contested usage*: both forms are common, one is safer with careful readers.

Who and whom follow the same pattern. Whom is the object form ("To whom did you speak?"), and it is fading from speech. Many editors now accept who in most positions except right after a preposition. Hopefully as a sentence adverb ("Hopefully, the bus is on time") was fought over for decades and is now accepted by nearly every guide. Data was once treated only as a plural ("the data are"), and many scientific journals still require it, while most general writing treats it as a mass noun ("the data is"). Literally has come to mean "figuratively" in casual speech ("I literally died"), and dictionaries record that sense, but in writing it still makes careful readers laugh at you, not with you.

Then there are the pairs that are not contested at all, only confused: affect (usually a verb) and effect (usually a noun); lie (to recline) and lay (to place); imply (the speaker hints) and infer (the listener concludes); *irregardless*, which dictionaries list as nonstandard and which no guide accepts in formal writing. These are not matters of taste. Getting them wrong in a letter is the kind of thing Priya notices.

For any usage you are unsure of, ask three questions. Is it contested, confused or simply a rule I never learned? Which way would the reader I am writing for lean? And can I *sidestep* it? "There are fewer errors" and "there are less errors" both vanish if you write "there are not as many errors." Sidestepping is not cheating. It is what professionals do when a fight is not worth having on the page.

words.d: a point of usage on which careful writers and guides genuinely disagree
a noun for something measured rather than counted, such as water, money or, in general writing, data
a nonstandard word meaning regardless; dictionaries list it, but formal writing avoids it
to rewrite a sentence so that a disputed usage question does not come up

look.title: The Sign at the Register
look.text: A supermarket in Evanston changed its express-lane signs from "10 items or less" to "10 items or fewer." Some shoppers praised it. Others said it sounded stuffy. A third group did not notice at all. The store manager later said the sign's only job was to keep the line moving.
look.prompt: Was the change worth making? Decide using the lesson's three questions, and say which group of shoppers the manager should care about most.

check.q: What makes a usage "contested" in this lesson's sense?
choices: It is always wrong
It appears only in speech
Both forms are in wide use, and careful readers disagree about which is acceptable
The dictionary does not list it
check.why: Contested usages are the ones on which authorities genuinely differ, unlike plain confusions.

check.q: Which pair is a plain confusion rather than a contested usage?
choices: less and fewer
who and whom
the data is and the data are
affect and effect
check.why: Affect and effect have distinct standard meanings; mixing them is an error, not a matter of taste.

check.q: What does the lesson mean by sidestepping?
choices: Rewriting so that the disputed choice does not arise
Leaving the sentence out
Using the nonstandard form on purpose
Looking up the word in two dictionaries
check.why: Sidestepping avoids the fight by finding a wording both sides accept.

lessons.title: Matching the Room
lessons.mainIdea: Register is the level of formality a writer chooses to fit the reader and the occasion, and shifting it on purpose is a skill, not a betrayal of your voice.
reading: Here is the same news three ways. To a friend: "got the job!!! start monday." To a teacher who wrote a recommendation: "I wanted to let you know I got the internship. Thank you for the letter; I start Monday." To the firm's human resources office: "I am writing to confirm that I accept the internship offer and will begin on Monday, June 8." Nothing in the first version is a mistake. It is the right *register* for a friend, and the third version would be strange sent to one. Register is the level of formality and the set of word choices a writer picks to fit the reader and the occasion.

Registers differ in predictable ways. *Informal* writing uses contractions, sentence fragments, slang, first names and whatever spelling the keyboard gives. *Formal* writing spells everything out, uses complete sentences, avoids slang, uses titles and last names until invited otherwise, and follows Standard English closely. In between sits most of college and work writing: complete sentences and standard usage, but a plain, human tone, with contractions allowed in many settings. The mistake students make most is not writing too casually. It is swinging so far toward formal that the writing goes stiff: "I am reaching out to inquire as to whether" instead of "I am writing to ask whether."

Most people already switch registers all day, between a coach, a grandparent and a group chat, without thinking about it. Linguists call the deliberate version of this *code-switching*, and it is a form of skill, not a loss of self. The trick in writing is to notice the switch and control it. Before you write anything that matters, name the reader and the room. Then choose three things on purpose: the greeting, the level of contractions and slang, and the closing. Get those three right and the rest of the register usually follows.

One warning about the middle register. Plain does not mean careless. "I'm writing to ask whether the position is still open" is plain and correct. "im writing to ask if the position is still open" is plain and, to a hiring manager, alarming. The capital I and the apostrophe cost nothing. They tell the reader that the plainness is a choice.

words.d: the level of formality and the word choices a writer uses to fit a reader and an occasion
casual language, with contractions, fragments and slang, suited to friends and private messages
careful, complete language following Standard English closely, suited to official or unfamiliar readers
shifting between language varieties or registers to fit the setting and the listener

look.title: One Message, Three Readers
look.text: You need to cancel a meeting tomorrow at 3:00. The readers: your best friend, your English teacher who agreed to review your college essay, and the manager at the store where you applied for a job. Each cancellation should be honest, brief and polite.
look.prompt: Write the greeting, one sentence and the closing for each reader. What exactly changes between the three, and what stays the same?

check.q: What is register?
choices: The list of words in a dictionary
The level of formality and word choices matched to the reader and occasion
The correct spelling of a word
The order of items in a list
check.why: Register is the writer's fit between language and setting.

check.q: According to the lesson, what is the most common register mistake students make?
choices: Writing too casually to friends
Using contractions in essays
Swinging so far toward formal that the writing goes stiff
Forgetting to sign their name
check.why: Overformal wording such as inquire as to whether is a bigger problem than casual tone.

check.q: Why does the lesson say "im writing to ask" alarms a hiring manager while "I'm writing to ask" does not?
choices: Because the second uses a formal verb
Because contractions are banned in email
Because the first is too long
Because the missing capital and apostrophe signal carelessness rather than a plain style chosen on purpose
check.why: Plainness is fine; visible carelessness is what costs credibility.

lessons.title: Email That Gets Answered
lessons.mainIdea: A good email has a subject line that says what it is, a greeting fitted to the reader, one clear request near the top, and a closing with your full name.
reading: Teachers, professors and managers get more email than they can read, and they sort it fast. The *subject line* is where the sorting happens. "Question" gets opened last. "Request to make up the Oct. 3 lab, Period 4" gets opened first and answered from memory. Make the subject line say what the email is about and, if possible, what you need. Then greet the reader by the name they use professionally: "Dear Ms. Okafor," or, once they have signed an email to you with a first name, "Hi Adaeze," is acceptable in most American workplaces.

The body should begin with the point. A common shape: one sentence that says who you are if the reader might not know, one sentence with the *request* or the news, then the details the reader needs to act, then thanks. Put the request near the top, not buried in paragraph three. Keep paragraphs short; on a phone, a six-line paragraph looks like a wall. If you are asking for something, make it easy to say yes: propose two times instead of asking "when works for you?" and attach what you say you attached, before you hit send.

Close with a *sign-off* that fits the register ("Thank you," "Best," "Sincerely,") and your full name. Add a class period or a job title if the reader may not place you. Then reread the whole thing once for tone. Email has no face and no voice, so a sentence that sounds direct in your head can sound angry on a screen. "I still have not received the form" reads as a complaint; "Could you let me know when the form is available?" asks the same thing and keeps the door open. That is *tone*, the attitude your words carry, and in email it is almost entirely made of word choice.

A few conventions that experienced people notice: one topic per email; reply within a day even if only to say when you will answer fully; never write in all capitals; never send an email you wrote angry without sleeping on it; and when you email a teacher or supervisor, remember that it can be forwarded, printed and read by someone you did not intend. Write what you would be comfortable seeing on a bulletin board.

words.d: the short title of an email that tells the reader what it is about before it is opened
the specific thing an email asks the reader to do, stated clearly near the top
the closing phrase and name that end an email, such as Sincerely, Maria Torres
the attitude a piece of writing carries toward its reader, made in email almost entirely by word choice

look.title: An Email That Works
look.text: Subject: Request to reschedule Thursday's interview. Dear Ms. Okafor, Thank you for offering me an interview for the summer internship. I am scheduled for Thursday at 2:00, but I have a state exam that afternoon that I cannot move. Would Wednesday at 2:00 or Friday at 10:00 work instead? I am glad to adjust to whatever is easiest for you. Thank you for your time. Sincerely, Marcus Bell, Lane Tech, Class of 2027
look.prompt: Find the four parts the lesson names: the subject line, the greeting, the request near the top and the sign-off. What makes the request easy to say yes to?

check.q: Which subject line does the lesson recommend?
choices: Request to make up the Oct. 3 lab, Period 4
Question
Hello
Important!!!
check.why: A subject line should say what the email is about and what is needed.

check.q: Where should the request go in an email?
choices: Near the top, after a sentence saying who you are
In the last paragraph
In the subject line only
In a separate email
check.why: Busy readers act on what they see first; a buried request is a missed request.

check.q: Why does the lesson prefer "Could you let me know when the form is available?" over "I still have not received the form"?
choices: It is shorter
It asks the same thing with a tone that keeps the door open
It uses a formal register
It avoids a contraction
check.why: Email tone is made of word choice, and a question reads as cooperative where a statement can read as a complaint.

lessons.title: Applications and Cover Letters
lessons.mainIdea: A cover letter is a short argument that you fit a specific job, written in a formal register, with every claim backed by a detail and every word checked.
reading: A *cover letter* is not a summary of your résumé. It is an argument, usually three or four paragraphs long, that a specific person should want you for a specific job. The first paragraph names the job and where you saw it and states, in one sentence, why you fit. The middle paragraph or two give evidence: not "I am hardworking" but "Last summer I framed nine houses with my uncle's crew, and I was the one who checked every measurement twice." The final paragraph asks for the interview, thanks the reader and says how to reach you. That is the whole form. Its power comes from specifics.

The *conventions* of the letter are fixed and are worth learning once. It is addressed to a named person when a name can be found; "Dear Hiring Manager" is the fallback, never "To whom it may concern." The register is formal: complete sentences, no slang, no contractions or very few, no jokes. It fits on one page. It uses the company's name and the job's title exactly as posted. It does not repeat the résumé line by line; it chooses the two or three things that matter for this job and explains them. And it is written fresh for each employer, because readers can smell a form letter in the first line.

Application forms have their own conventions. Fill every field, even the ones that seem redundant; a blank looks like carelessness. Use the same spelling of your name everywhere. Write in complete sentences where a box asks for sentences, and in short phrases where it asks for a list. Give an email address that is a version of your name, not a joke you made in seventh grade. And *proofread* the form the way you would a letter, because it is read by the same person.

Marcus's letter failed on one word, and that is the last convention: a cover letter is judged more strictly than almost anything else you will write, because its whole purpose is to show what you are like when you are trying your hardest. Read it aloud. Read it backward, sentence by sentence, so that your eye stops sliding. Have someone else read it. Then wait an hour and read it once more. A letter with zero errors is not a sign of genius. It is a sign of care, and care is what the reader is hiring.

words.d: a short formal letter sent with an application that argues you fit a specific job
the customs a kind of writing is expected to follow, such as a letter's greeting, length and register
to read a finished text slowly, looking only for errors in spelling, punctuation and usage

look.title: Marcus's Second Letter, Middle Paragraph
look.text: Last summer I worked on my uncle's framing crew, where I was responsible for checking every measurement before a wall went up. On one job I caught a three-quarter-inch error on a header that would have thrown off the second floor. In my community college drafting class, I earned the highest score on the final plan set. I would bring the same habit of checking small things to your team's drawings.
look.prompt: Each sentence backs a claim with a detail. Rewrite the paragraph as the vague version most applicants send, then explain what the reader loses.

check.q: What is the job of the middle paragraphs of a cover letter?
choices: To list every job on the résumé
To give specific evidence that the writer fits this job
To explain why the writer left the last job
To describe the writer's hobbies
check.why: The letter is an argument, and the middle paragraphs supply the evidence.

check.q: Which greeting does the lesson call the fallback when no name can be found?
choices: Hey there,
To whom it may concern,
Dear Hiring Manager,
Dear Sir,
check.why: A named person is best; Dear Hiring Manager is the accepted fallback.

check.q: Why does the lesson say a cover letter is judged more strictly than most writing?
choices: Because it is longer than an essay
Because employers are grammar experts
Because it is written in italics
Because its whole purpose is to show what the writer is like when trying hardest
check.why: The letter is a sample of the writer's care, so an error argues against the writer.

lessons.title: Errors That Cost Credibility
lessons.mainIdea: A short list of errors, mostly involving apostrophes, homophones and agreement, does most of the damage to a writer's credibility, and each one can be checked with a simple test.
reading: Read this paragraph from a company's proposal, written for this lesson with its errors left in. "Our team is proud of it's record this year. There were three project's finished ahead of schedule, and the client's said they were more satisfied then last year. Each of the managers have signed off. We hope you will choose us for you're next project, its the right move." Four sentences, seven errors. A reader who catches even two of them stops trusting the numbers in the rest of the proposal. That is what *credibility* means: the reader's willingness to believe you, and it is spent one small error at a time.

Four of the seven are apostrophe errors, and apostrophes cause more trouble than any other mark. The *apostrophe* does two jobs: it shows possession (the client's office) and it marks missing letters in a contraction (it's for it is). It never makes a plural. "Three projects" and "the clients" take no apostrophe. The test for its and it's is to say "it is" out loud in the sentence: "proud of it is record" fails, so the word is its. The same test works for you're (you are), they're (they are) and who's (who is).

The *homophones* come next: then and than, there, their and they're, to, too and two, affect and effect, loose and lose. Than compares (more satisfied than last year); then tells time. "Could of" is not English; the phrase is could have, which sounds like could've in speech. *Agreement* errors hide when a phrase comes between the subject and the verb: "Each of the managers have signed" should be "has," because the subject is each, not managers. Cover the phrase between subject and verb and read what is left.

Here is the same paragraph repaired. "Our team is proud of its record this year. Three projects finished ahead of schedule, and the clients said they were more satisfied than last year. Each of the managers has signed off. We hope you will choose us for your next project; it's the right move." Nothing about the content changed. Everything about the writer changed.

words.d: a reader's willingness to believe a writer, which small errors reduce
the mark that shows possession or missing letters in a contraction; it never forms a plural
words that sound alike but are spelled differently and mean different things, such as their and there
the match between a subject and its verb in number, as in each manager has, the managers have

look.title: Seven Errors in Four Sentences
look.cite: counted for this lesson in the proposal paragraph in the reading
look.prompt: More than half the errors involve one mark. If you could teach a coworker a single test in one minute, which would prevent the most damage?

check.q: What test tells you whether to write its or it's?
choices: Say "it is" in the sentence; if it works, use it's
Count the syllables
Check whether the next word is a noun
Use it's for possession
check.why: It's is only ever a contraction of it is or it has; its is the possessive.

check.q: Why is "Each of the managers have signed off" wrong?
choices: Because managers should be manager
Because the subject is each, which takes has
Because of should be off
Because signed should be signs
check.why: The phrase of the managers sits between the subject and the verb; the subject each is singular.

check.q: What does the lesson mean by credibility?
choices: The length of a proposal
The formality of the register
The reader's willingness to believe the writer
The number of sources cited
check.why: Credibility is trust, and small errors spend it.

lessons.title: The Ten-Minute Edit
lessons.mainIdea: When time is short, edit in passes with a fixed order: meaning first, then the personal error list, then the mechanical checks, then a final read aloud.
reading: The essay is due at midnight and it is 11:40. Or the form must be submitted before the office closes. Editing under pressure is a skill of its own, and it is mostly a matter of order. Most people, given ten minutes, read from the top and fix whatever they happen to notice. That catches the errors in the first paragraph and almost none in the last. A better plan is to make several fast *passes*, each one looking for one thing, so your eye does not have to hold everything at once.

Pass one, three minutes: meaning. Read only the first sentence of every paragraph. Does the piece still make the argument you meant, in the order you meant? Fix any paragraph whose first sentence does not match its job. Pass two, three minutes: your own *error list*. Every writer has three or four errors they make over and over; yours might be its/it's, run-on sentences and dropped words. Keep the list in your notes and search for those errors only. A word processor's find function can hunt for "it's" and " then " in seconds.

Pass three, two minutes: the *mechanical* checks that do not need judgment. Names spelled the same everywhere. Titles marked consistently. Every quotation with a citation. Every citation in the works cited. Numbers that match between the text and any table. The spell-checker run once, with each flag actually read, since it will not catch a correct word in the wrong place. Pass four, two minutes: read the last two paragraphs aloud, slowly, because that is where tired writers leave the most mistakes. Then stop.

Under real pressure, the last skill is knowing what to skip. A sentence that is clumsy but clear can stay. A sentence whose meaning a reader could miss cannot. When you must choose between polishing a phrase and checking whether your citation page matches your quotations, check the citations; the *stakes* are higher. Editing is triage. Fix what would cost you the most, in the order it would cost you, and let the rest wait for a draft you have time for.

words.d: one read-through of a draft looking for a single kind of problem
a writer's personal list of the mistakes they make most often, used to target editing
describing checks that follow fixed rules and need no judgment, such as spelling names consistently
what a writer stands to lose if a particular error is missed

look.title: Eleven Forty
look.text: A student has twenty minutes before a history paper is due. She knows she tends to write comma splices and to type "then" for "than." Her paper has six quotations, a works cited page and a conclusion she wrote fast. She usually starts editing by rereading her introduction, which she has already revised four times.
look.prompt: Plan her twenty minutes in passes. Which part of her usual habit is wasting time, and where are her stakes highest?

check.q: Why does the lesson recommend editing in passes?
choices: Because passes are faster than reading once
Because errors only occur in the first paragraph
Because spell-checkers require it
Because looking for one thing at a time lets the eye catch more than trying to hold everything at once
check.why: Each pass has a single target, which is more reliable than one general read.

check.q: What is a personal error list?
choices: A list of the three or four mistakes a writer makes most often, used to target a pass
The teacher's rubric
The list of comments on a graded paper
A dictionary of common errors
check.why: Writers repeat their own mistakes, so knowing them makes a fast pass effective.

check.q: With time for only one, which should a writer check first, and why?
choices: A clumsy phrase, because style matters most
The citation page against the quotations, because the stakes are higher
The font, because readers notice it first
The title, because it is read first
check.why: Editing under pressure is triage: fix what would cost the most.

lessons.title: Settling a Usage Question
lessons.mainIdea: A usage question is settled by consulting the right reference in the right order: the dictionary for words, the style guide for format, a usage guide for disputes, and real examples for what writers actually do.
reading: You are writing a lab report and you cannot remember whether it is "comprised of" or "composed of," whether "data" takes "is" or "are," and whether the abbreviation for milliliters takes a period. Three questions, three different tools. Guessing is the fourth option, and it is the one most students take. Learning which *reference* answers which kind of question takes an hour and pays off for life.

For the meaning, spelling and standard forms of a word, the tool is a *dictionary*, and for American writers the one most publishers use is Merriam-Webster, which is free online. Its entries also carry usage notes on disputed words; look up "comprise" and you will find the whole argument summarized in a paragraph. For format questions, such as how to abbreviate units, how to cite or when to spell out numbers, the tool is your style guide: MLA for most English classes, APA for psychology and the sciences, Chicago for books, AP for journalism. Most school libraries have them, and the guides' own websites answer common questions for free.

For a genuine dispute, when the dictionary says "some object" and you need to know how much they object, the tool is a *usage guide*, a book organized by the disputed words. Garner's Modern English Usage and Merriam-Webster's Dictionary of English Usage are the two most respected American ones, and they often disagree with each other, which is itself informative. The last tool is real evidence: a *corpus*, a large searchable collection of actual published writing. The Corpus of Contemporary American English, built by a linguist at Brigham Young University and free online, lets you see how often "the data is" appears in academic writing versus magazines. That is the descriptive view made practical.

The order matters. Dictionary, then style guide, then usage guide, then corpus. Stop as soon as you have an answer that satisfies your reader; most questions end at the first or second step. And write down what you decided in your style sheet so that you never look it up twice for the same paper. A writer who knows where to look is never stuck for more than two minutes.

words.d: a book or website consulted for facts, such as a dictionary or style guide
a reference that gives a word's spelling, meanings, pronunciation and often a note on its usage
a reference organized by disputed words that explains each dispute and advises writers
a large searchable collection of real texts used to see how words are actually used

look.title: Three Questions, Three Tools
look.text: A student's questions during one evening: (1) Is it "alright" or "all right" in an essay? (2) Does the MLA want the year or the page number in a parenthetical citation? (3) Her teacher marked "very unique" as wrong; is that fair, and do published writers use it?
look.prompt: Match each question to the tool that answers it, and say what the student should do if the first tool she checks gives no clear answer.

check.q: Which reference answers a question about how to abbreviate a unit in a lab report?
choices: The style guide for the field
A corpus
A thesaurus
A usage guide
check.why: Format questions belong to the style guide; the dictionary handles words, the usage guide handles disputes.

check.q: What does a corpus let a writer see?
choices: The correct rule for a word
How often and where a form actually appears in real writing
The origin of a word
The teacher's preference
check.why: A corpus is evidence of usage, the descriptive view in practice.

check.q: What order does the lesson give for consulting references?
choices: Corpus, usage guide, dictionary, style guide
Style guide, corpus, dictionary, usage guide
Dictionary, style guide, usage guide, corpus
Usage guide first, then whichever is nearest
check.why: Start with the fastest, most common answer and go deeper only if needed.

lessons.title: Language Variety
lessons.mainIdea: Every variety of English, including African American English and the Englishes of bilingual communities, has consistent grammar; Standard English is one variety among many, expected in certain settings.
reading: Chicago speaks in many Englishes. A grandmother on the South Side may say "She be working late," using a form that African American English uses to mark a habit, something that happens regularly, which Standard English cannot say in a single verb. A student in Pilsen may say "I have twelve years" the first month after arriving from Mexico, carrying the Spanish way of stating age into English. A teenager on the Northwest Side says "gym shoes" where a New Yorker says "sneakers." Each of these is a *dialect* or variety of English: a full system with its own rules, sounds and words, shared by a community.

Linguists established decades ago that nonstandard varieties are not broken Standard English. *African American English*, sometimes called African American Vernacular English, has consistent grammar. "She be working" and "She working" mean different things, habitual and right now, and a speaker never confuses them. That grammar has been studied in universities since the 1960s and is the subject of hundreds of books. Calling a variety "bad English" is a social judgment, not a linguistic one, in exactly the way that calling one accent "no accent" is. Everyone has an accent. Everyone speaks a dialect.

None of this makes Standard English unnecessary. It is the variety of the classroom, the courtroom, the cover letter and most published writing, and a student who cannot produce it on demand is shut out of rooms they deserve to enter. The point is what kind of thing it is. Standard English is a register and a variety, not the language itself, and learning it is *addition*, not correction. A student who speaks African American English at home and writes Standard English in a lab report is doing what a bilingual person does. That is more skill, not less.

For the writer, two practical rules follow. First, in a setting that expects Standard English, use it, and use it well; the reader is not wrong to expect it. Second, never treat another person's variety as a sign of intelligence or effort. In dialogue, in a quotation or in a profile, render a person's speech accurately and respectfully, and do not "correct" a quotation into a dialect the speaker did not use. A writer who understands variety is harder to fool and kinder on the page.

words.d: a variety of a language, with its own consistent grammar, sounds and words, shared by a community
a variety of English spoken in many Black American communities, with its own consistent grammar
describing an action that happens regularly, which some varieties mark with a special verb form
the view that learning Standard English adds a variety to what a student already has rather than replacing it

look.title: Two Sentences, Two Meanings
look.text: A teacher hears a student say, "My brother be at the library," and later, "My brother at the library." She assumes both are careless versions of "My brother is at the library." A classmate explains that the first means he is usually there and the second means he is there right now.
look.prompt: What did the teacher's assumption cause her to miss, and how should that change the way she responds to the student's writing in Standard English settings?

check.q: What does the reading say about African American English?
choices: It has no rules
It is a mixture of errors
It is used only in speech
It has consistent grammar that has been studied in universities for decades
check.why: Linguists have documented its grammar; it is a variety, not broken Standard English.

check.q: In the lesson's view, what kind of thing is Standard English?
choices: One variety among many, expected in certain settings
The only correct form of the language
The variety with no accent
A dialect spoken only in schools
check.why: Standard English is a register and variety with social power, not the language itself.

check.q: What does the lesson mean by calling the learning of Standard English addition?
choices: Students add extra words to sentences
It adds a variety to what a student already speaks rather than replacing it
It adds points to a grade
It is added to the curriculum in eleventh grade
check.why: Learning the standard variety is like becoming bilingual, a gain rather than a correction.

lessons.title: Respect on the Page
lessons.mainIdea: Respectful usage means calling people and groups what they call themselves, getting names and titles right, and choosing words that describe rather than judge.
reading: A reporter spells a source's name wrong, and the source never trusts the newspaper again. A form lists a student as "Jonathan" when he has gone by "Jon" his whole life. A letter opens "Dear Sirs" to an office run by three women. None of these is a grammar error, yet each one costs the writer more credibility than a comma splice, because each says the writer did not look. Respect in usage starts with *accuracy about people*: their names, spelled as they spell them; their titles, as they hold them; their pronouns, as they state them.

Names for groups follow the same principle. Use the term a group uses for itself, and know that these terms change. Most American style guides now capitalize Black when referring to people; they are divided on White. Native American, American Indian and Indigenous are all in use, and the most respectful choice is often the specific nation, such as Potawatomi, whose people lived where Chicago now stands. Latino, Latina, Hispanic and the newer Latinx are used by different people for different reasons; the AP Stylebook notes that Latinx is not widely used by the people it describes. When in doubt, ask, or follow the usage of the community's own institutions.

*Person-first language* ("a student with a disability") was the standard for decades; some communities, including many autistic and Deaf people, prefer identity-first language ("an autistic student"). Neither is wrong. The respectful move is to use what the person or community prefers, and, when writing about individuals, to mention a disability, a religion or an origin only when it is relevant to the point. That last rule, *relevance*, does most of the work. A sentence that mentions a person's background when it has nothing to do with the story tells the reader more about the writer than about the subject.

Finally, the *generic masculine*, using he and man to mean everyone, was standard until the 1970s and is now avoided by every major guide. Write "a nurse should wash her hands" only if the nurse is a specific woman; otherwise recast in the plural ("nurses should wash their hands"), use singular they or repeat the noun. None of this is about fear of offending. It is the same discipline as every other lesson in this unit: knowing who the reader is, and choosing the words that let the reader see the subject clearly instead of seeing the writer's assumptions.

words.d: getting names, titles and stated pronouns exactly right, as the first form of respect in writing
phrasing that names the person before a condition, as in a student with a disability
the test of whether a detail about a person's background belongs in the sentence at all
the older practice of using he and man to refer to people in general, now avoided by major guides

look.title: The Profile Draft
look.text: A student's profile of a school custodian begins: "Mr. Reyes, a Mexican immigrant who speaks broken English, has kept the building clean for nineteen years." Mr. Reyes was born in Texas, prefers to be called Ray, and speaks two languages. The profile's subject is the building's history.
look.prompt: Using the lesson's rules of accuracy and relevance, rewrite the opening sentence and explain each change.

check.q: According to the lesson, what is the first form of respect in writing about people?
choices: Using formal register
Avoiding all personal details
Getting names, titles and stated pronouns exactly right
Using person-first language always
check.why: Accuracy about people, starting with names, shows the writer looked.

check.q: What does the relevance test ask?
choices: Whether the sentence is grammatically complete
Whether the reader knows the person
Whether the term is capitalized
Whether a detail about a person's background has anything to do with the point
check.why: A background detail that does not serve the point reveals the writer's assumptions rather than the subject.

check.q: Which sentence avoids the generic masculine?
choices: Nurses should wash their hands before every visit.
A nurse should wash his hands before every visit.
Every man on the staff should wash his hands.
A nurse, he should wash his hands.
check.why: Recasting in the plural refers to everyone without assuming a gender.

review.q: Which statement is descriptive rather than prescriptive?
choices: Never end a sentence with a preposition.
Most American speakers end questions with prepositions, as in Where are you from?
Use fewer with countable nouns.
Avoid irregardless in formal writing.
review.why: It reports what speakers do rather than telling writers what to do.

review.q: Why does the chapter say the split-infinitive rule was never solid?
choices: Because Latin had many split infinitives
Because no one has ever split an infinitive
Because it was borrowed from Latin grammar, and English writers had split infinitives for centuries
Because the AP Stylebook invented it
review.why: The rule was a Latin import, not a fact about English.

review.q: What is the most common register mistake the chapter names for school and work writing?
choices: Using contractions
Writing too casually
Forgetting a subject line
Going so formal that the writing turns stiff
review.why: Overformal wording is a bigger problem than plain, correct language.

review.q: Which cover-letter sentence follows the chapter's advice?
choices: Last summer I checked every measurement on a nine-house framing job and caught a header error before the wall went up.
I am a hard worker with great attention to detail.
I would be an asset to you're team.
To whom it may concern, I want a job.
review.why: Specific evidence beats a general claim, and the sentence is error-free.

choices: The clients said its the right move.
The clients said it's the right move.
The client's said its the right move.
The clients' said it's the right move.
review.why: Clients is a plain plural with no apostrophe, and it's is the contraction of it is.

review.q: In the ten-minute edit, what comes first?
choices: Running the spell-checker
Reading the introduction again
Checking meaning by reading the first sentence of every paragraph
Reading the conclusion aloud
review.why: Meaning comes first; mechanical passes follow.

review.q: A writer wants to know how often "the data is" appears in published academic writing. Which tool answers that?
choices: A dictionary
A style guide
A thesaurus
A corpus
review.why: A corpus is a searchable collection of real texts that shows actual usage.

review.q: How does the chapter describe the relationship between African American English and Standard English?
choices: Both are varieties with consistent grammar; Standard English is the one expected in certain settings
One is correct and the other is a set of errors
They are the same variety with different accents
Standard English has no grammar rules
review.why: Every variety has rules; Standard English is a register with social power, learned as an addition.
